01.event: Rabbi Elazar moved to Eretz Yisrael, was ordained, and was seated on the calendar council, remarking at each step that he had been spared a curse.
01.turn: Each milestone showed that one of three curses from Ezekiel's prophecy did not apply to him.
01.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael he said he had been spared one curse. When he was ordained he said two, and when he was seated on the council of the calendar he said three. The verse in Ezekiel names these three as punishments for false prophets, and he avoided them all.
01.missing: Little narrative action; mostly three remarks tied to a verse.

04.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
04.event: They meant to act on a baraita letting a nursing mother remarry at once, but an old woman said Rav Nahman had forbidden it to her.
04.turn: Rav Pappi showed from a baraita and Shmuel's rule that the stricter ruling applies; the two said they had not thought of it.
04.outcome: They accepted it; the halakha was set that if the child died she may remarry, but if weaned she may not.
04.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna were about to permit a woman with a nursing child to remarry immediately, following a baraita. An old woman told them Rav Nahman had once forbidden it to her, and Rav Pappi argued from another baraita and a ruling of Shmuel that the restriction stands. They admitted they had overlooked it, and the final ruling was a compromise.

05.event: Ravina arranged his son's marriage and recited the wedding blessing from the betrothal, trusting the bride's family would not back out.
05.turn: The bride's family retracted and the wedding was cancelled.
05.summary: Ravina arranged a match for his son with the house of Rav Haviva and began reciting the wedding blessing from the betrothal, saying he was sure they would not retract. It did not work out and they retracted, so the wedding never happened.

06.event: Rav Safra objected to Rava that the Tigris separated Akistefon and Ardeshir by more than the permitted distance, so they should not count as one city.
06.turn: Rava went out and showed him the foundations of a wall submerged in the Tigris.
06.outcome: The objection was answered: the cities were in fact linked.
06.summary: Rav Safra challenged Rava, pointing out that a river separates the two cities that are treated as one. Rava took him outside and showed him the remains of a wall under the water that joined them, answering the challenge.

07.event: His colleagues criticized Ben Azzai for teaching the duty to have children without marrying himself, and he answered that his soul yearned for Torah.
07.turn: He defended himself by saying others can sustain the world.
07.summary: The Sages told Ben Azzai that he preached procreation well but did not practice it. He replied that his soul was drawn to Torah and the world can be kept going by others.
07.missing: A short exchange rather than a full event.

08.event: The Rabbis urged Rav Sheshet to marry and have sons, and he answered that his daughter's sons were his sons.
08.turn: The Gemara explains he was merely putting them off, since he had become impotent from Rav Huna's long discourses.
08.outcome: His real reason was revealed, not a legal view.
08.summary: The Rabbis told Rav Sheshet to marry and father sons, and he replied that his daughter's sons count as his own. The Gemara says he was only deflecting them, because he had become impotent from sitting through Rav Huna's long lectures.
08.missing: Brief anecdote embedded in legal argument.

09.actor: A man who left a divorce condition and his arrival
09.event: A man told agents holding his wife's get that it would take effect if he did not return within thirty days, and he arrived at the end of the thirty days but was stopped by the ferry on the far side of the river.
09.turn: He shouted across that he had come, but Shmuel said this was not a return.
09.outcome: The condition was treated as unmet, so the get took effect.
09.summary: A man gave a conditional divorce that would take effect if he did not come back in thirty days. He reached the river at the end of the period but the ferry was on the other side, so he called out that he had come. Shmuel ruled that this did not count as returning.

10.actor: Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda and Rabba
10.event: A divorce document dated by the governor of Bascar was sent by Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda to Rabba with a question.
10.turn: Rabba replied that even Rabbi Meir would accept it.
10.summary: A bill of divorce had been dated by the years of the governor of Bascar. Rav Nahman sent it to Rabba to ask whether this was valid, and Rabba answered that even Rabbi Meir would allow it because the governor belonged to the same kingdom.
10.missing: It is a legal query and reply; the case itself is barely told.

11.actor: A man sent by his father to fetch chicks
11.event: At his father's request he climbed to the roof, sent away the mother bird and took the young, thus doing two mitzvot.
11.turn: On his way back he fell and died, though both mitzvot promise long life.
11.outcome: The reward is understood to belong to the world to come.
11.summary: A man's father told him to go up to a building and bring chicks. He climbed up, sent off the mother bird and took the young, and on the way down he fell and died. The question of where his promised long life went was answered by saying the reward is in the world that is entirely good.

12.actor: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and the Elders
12.event: Elders gathered in a loft in Lod were asked whether study or action is greater.
12.turn: Rabbi Tarfon said action, Rabbi Akiva said study, and then everyone agreed on study.
12.outcome: They concluded study is greater because it leads to action.
12.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were reclining in a loft in Lod when asked whether study or action is greater. Rabbi Tarfon answered action and Rabbi Akiva answered study; all of them then agreed that study is greater since it leads to action.

13.event: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter betrothed the shepherd Akiva and sent him to study, and her father disowned her.
13.turn: Akiva returned after twelve years with thousands of students, then went off for twelve more at her urging; on his second return her father came to ask him to annul his vow.
13.outcome: Her father learned who he was and gave Akiva half his money; the wife's recognition was honored.
13.summary: Akiva was a shepherd when his employer's daughter saw his worth, betrothed him privately and sent him to study. Her father cut her off. Akiva came back after twelve years with twelve thousand students, overheard that she would be left alone, and went away for another twelve. He returned with twenty-four thousand students and she met him, and when her father came asking him to annul his vow, Akiva revealed himself and the father gave him half his money.

14.event: The Sages told Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to marry and have children, and he answered that if he had merited he would already have had them.
14.turn: The Gemara says he was only putting them off, being impotent from Rav Huna's discourse.
14.summary: The Sages urged Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to remarry and have children and he said that if he had merited it he would already have had them. The Gemara explains he was deflecting them, because he had become impotent from Rav Huna's long lectures.
14.missing: A short anecdote used only as a proof in a legal argument.

15.actor: Rabban Gamliel and the sages Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok
15.event: At the wedding of Rabban Gamliel's son, Rabban Gamliel stood and served drinks to the sages.
15.turn: Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup while Rabbi Yehoshua accepted it, and Eliezer protested.
15.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua cited Abraham and Rabbi Tzadok cited God to show that a leader may serve guests.
15.summary: Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi, stood and served drinks to Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok at his son's wedding. Eliezer would not take the cup and objected when Yehoshua did. Yehoshua pointed to Abraham serving his guests, and Tzadok said God Himself serves all, so Gamliel's serving was acceptable.

16.event: Rabbi Yosei met Elijah the prophet and asked how a wife helps a man.
16.turn: Elijah answered with the example of raw wheat and flax that a wife turns into bread and clothing.
16.outcome: Rabbi Yosei was told that a wife lights his eyes and stands him on his feet.
16.summary: Rabbi Yosei came across Elijah and asked what the verse means that a woman helps her husband. Elijah answered that a man brings home wheat and flax he cannot eat or wear raw, and his wife turns them into food and clothing.

17.actor: A woman who gave her property to her daughter
17.event: A woman about to marry wrote her property over to her daughter to keep it from her future husband, then was married and divorced.
17.turn: She claimed the property back; Rav Nahman tore up the deed, Rav Anan complained to Mar Ukva, and Mar Ukva said Shmuel too would tear such a document.
17.outcome: Rav Nahman's tearing of the deed was upheld.
17.summary: A woman wrote her property over to her daughter so her husband could not reach it, then married and was divorced. She went to Rav Nahman, who tore up the document. Rav Anan complained about this to Mar Ukva, but after hearing the facts Mar Ukva said that Shmuel would also tear such a document of evasion.

18.actor: A man who sold his property to ascend to Eretz Yisrael
18.event: A man sold his property in order to go up to Eretz Yisrael but in the end did not go.
18.turn: Rav Ashi gave a ruling on whether he can cancel the sale.
18.outcome: The sale stood, with a version distinguishing cases of unavoidable obstacles.
18.summary: A man sold his property with the intention of going to Eretz Yisrael but never went. Rav Ashi said that if he had wanted to he could have gone, so the sale stands, with a second version leaving room for the case where he was prevented on the way.
18.missing: Case is only sketched; the passage is mostly about the ruling.

19.event: For two and a half years the two schools disagreed over whether it would have been better for man not to have been created.
19.outcome: They concluded it would have been better not to be created, but now he should examine his deeds.
19.summary: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argued for two and a half years about whether man was better off created or not. They finally took a vote and decided it would be better not to have been created, but since he exists he should examine his actions.
19.missing: A dispute and its resolution, not a story of individuals.

20.event: A man told those at his bedside that his property should go to Toviya, then died, and Toviya came to claim it.
20.turn: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that Toviya had come.
20.summary: A man said his property should go to Toviya and then died. When Toviya showed up, Rabbi Yohanan said that Toviya had come, meaning he gets the property.
20.missing: The case is stated briefly; the ruling is the point.
